960	### 12.3 What `kill` cannot do
961	
962	`kill` does **not** flip a cancellation token in a running deadreckon process. If a deadreckon `run` is still executing, `kill` only signals its child PIDs; the deadreckon process itself relies on its own cancellation token tree, which `kill` doesn't reach across processes. In practice this works because killing the children causes the providers/sandbox to error out, which the turn loop sees and propagates as a failure — but the seam is not as clean as it could be (this is named in the robustness rider as a hardening target).
963	
964	---
965	
966	## 13. Acceptance Gate & Anti-Self-Attestation
967	
968	### 13.1 The principle
969	
970	The agent (LLM) **cannot** be trusted to declare a run done. `Completed` is reachable only via an acceptance marker signed by an external binary that the agent does not have keys to.
971	
972	### 13.2 `AcceptanceMarker`
973	
974	`crates/deadreckon-core/src/gate.rs:16-28`:
975	
976	```rust
977	pub struct AcceptanceMarker {
978	    pub schema_version: u32,
979	    pub run_id: String,
980	    pub status: String,           // "pass" | "fail"
981	    pub produced_by: String,      // must be "dr-gate"
982	    pub checked_at: DateTime<Utc>,
983	    pub working_dir: PathBuf,
984	    pub signature: String,        // hash over fields + nonce
985	    pub check_count: usize,
986	}
987	```
988	
989	Marker location: `<run_root>/proofs/turn-acceptance.json`.
990	
991	### 13.3 `dr-gate` binary
992	
993	`crates/deadreckon/src/bin/dr-gate.rs` (33 lines). Standalone binary that:
994	
995	1. Reads `--run <id>` and `--working-dir <path>`.
996	2. Loads `acceptance.yaml` (if present) from the run root.
997	3. Runs each check (cargo test, file-exists, content-match, build-success).
998	4. If all required checks pass, writes a signed `AcceptanceMarker` to `proofs/turn-acceptance.json`.
999	
1000	The marker's `signature` is computed from `gate/nonce` (a UUID written at run-init time by the deadreckon binary at `state.rs:188`). Only `dr-gate` reads the nonce; the agent never has access.
1001	
1002	### 13.4 Validation
1003	
1004	`gate.rs:88-118`:
1005	
1006	```rust
1007	pub fn validate_acceptance_marker(state: &PipelineState) -> Result<AcceptanceMarker> {
1008	    let path = marker_path(state);
1009	    let raw = std::fs::read(&path).with_path(&path)?;
1010	    let marker: AcceptanceMarker = serde_json::from_slice(&raw).with_json_path(&path)?;
1011	    if marker.schema_version != 1 { return Err(...); }
1012	    if marker.run_id != state.run_id {
1013	        return Err("acceptance marker run_id ... does not match");
1014	    }
1015	    if marker.status != "pass" || marker.produced_by != "dr-gate" {
1016	        return Err("acceptance marker was not produced by dr-gate with pass status");
1017	    }
1018	    let expected = marker_signature(&state.run_root, &marker)?;
1019	    if marker.signature != expected {
1020	        return Err("acceptance marker signature is invalid; forged self-attestation refused");
1021	    }
1022	    Ok(marker)
1023	}
1024	```
1025	
1026	A forged marker by the agent fails the signature check at line 114.
1027	
1028	### 13.5 Where the gate is invoked
1029	
1030	The CLI sub-agent path and regular Done path in `crates/deadreckon-runtime/src/turn_loop.rs` both call:
1031	
1032	```rust
1033	run_acceptance_gate(state)?;
1034	validate_acceptance_marker(state)?;
1035	promote_if_ready(state)?;
1036	```
1037	
1038	The first call invokes `dr-gate` as a subprocess. The second validates what `dr-gate` wrote. The third atomically swaps the working tree into the library.
1039	
1040	Failure at any step prevents the run from reaching `Completed`.
1041	
1042	---
1043	
1044	## 14. Telemetry: Spend, Traces, Provenance, Events
1045	
1046	Four append-only JSONL files capture every run's history. All live under `<run_root>/`. All written via `append_json_line` (`state.rs:375-388`), which opens in append mode and `sync_all`s after each line.
1047	
1048	### 14.1 `spend.jsonl`
1049	
1050	Schema:
1051	
1052	```json
1053	{
1054	  "timestamp": "<RFC3339>",
1055	  "run_id": "...",
1056	  "turn": 3,
1057	  "provider": "cli:claude-code",
1058	  "model": "claude-sonnet-4-5",
1059	  "input_tokens": 0,
1060	  "output_tokens": 0,
1061	  "cost_usd": 0.0,
1062	  "subscription": true,
1063	  "wall_time_seconds": 42.1
1064	}
1065	```
1066	
1067	One line per LLM call. HTTP providers fill in token counts and USD; CLI providers fill in `subscription: true` + `wall_time_seconds`.
1068	
1069	### 14.2 `traces.jsonl`
1070	
1071	Schema:
1072	
1073	```json
1074	{
1075	  "timestamp": "<RFC3339>",
1076	  "run_id": "...",
1077	  "turn": 3,
1078	  "event": "llm.complete" | "tool.bash" | "tool.write_file" | "tool.cli_subagent" | "import.claude-code" | ...,
1079	  "latency_ms": 1234,
1080	  "detail": { "tool_call_id": "...", "provider": "...", "trace": {...} }
1081	}
1082	```
1083	
1084	Every LLM call, every tool dispatch, every notable event. The detail block carries free-form JSON per event kind.
1085	
1086	### 14.3 `provenance.jsonl`
1087	
1088	Schema (per file changed):
1089	
1090	```json
1091	{
1092	  "timestamp": "<RFC3339>",
1093	  "run_id": "...",
1094	  "turn": 3,
1095	  "tool_call_id": "...",
1096	  "model": "claude-sonnet-4-5",
1097	  "session_id": "...",
1098	  "file": "src/main.rs"
1099	}
1100	```
1101	
1102	One line per file changed by a tool call. Lets `show <run-id>` answer "which prompt produced this file?"
1103	
1104	### 14.4 `events.jsonl`
1105	
1106	Structured `RunEvent` log: `TurnStarted { turn }`, `ToolCallStarted { tool_call_id, kind }`, `ToolCallResult { tool_call_id, status, latency_ms }`, `RunCompleted { outcome }`. Also published on a `tokio::sync::broadcast` channel (`events.rs`) for in-process subscribers (the TUI uses this when implemented; today the TUI polls files instead — see §22).
1107	
1108	---
1109	
1110	## 15. Resume Semantics
1111	
1112	`crates/deadreckon/src/main.rs:940-1000` is the `resume_command` handler.
1113	
1114	### 15.1 The Completed guard
1115	
1116	`main.rs:947`:
1117	
1118	```rust
1119	if state.status == RunStatus::Completed {
1120	    println!("run {} is already completed", state.run_id);
1121	    return Ok(());
1122	}
1123	```
1124	
1125	Completed runs cannot be resumed. They can be re-promoted (idempotent) but not re-entered into the loop. The only forward path for a completed run today is to start a new run.
1126	
1127	### 15.2 The replay process
1128	
1129	For non-Completed runs (`Failed`, `Killed`, `Paused`):
1130	
1131	1. Acquire the task lock.
1132	2. Clear `failure_reason`, `pause_reason`, `killed_at`.
1133	3. Set `status = Planned`.
1134	4. Optionally extend `max_wall_seconds` from the resume flag.
1135	5. Set `child_pids = vec![cli_pid]`.
1136	6. `save_state()`.
1137	7. Call `run_turn_loop` with `RunLoopConfig.from_turn = <CLI flag>`.
1138	8. The loop calls `load_or_reconstruct_history(state, from_turn)` in `crates/deadreckon-runtime/src/turn_loop.rs`, which loads `history.json` if present, else reconstructs from `traces.jsonl`. With `from_turn = N`, history is truncated to N entries and `state.turn = N`.
1139	
1140	History reconstruction tolerates a `traces.jsonl` that ends mid-tool-call by ignoring incomplete entries — the next turn re-runs that turn.
1141	
1142	See `/Users/gdc/deadreckon/docs/RESUME-SEMANTICS.md` for the contract.
1143	
1144	---
1145	
1146	## 16. Cross-Tool Import
1147	
1148	`deadreckon import <source>` reads from external coding-agent histories and synthesizes a deadreckon run from them. Today's coverage:
1149	
1150	| Source | Path (overridable via env) | Format |
1151	|---|---|---|
1152	| `claude-code` | `~/.claude/projects/` (`DEADRECKON_IMPORT_CLAUDE_ROOT`) | JSONL |

1154	| `cursor` | `~/.cursor/chats/` (`DEADRECKON_IMPORT_CURSOR_ROOT`) | SQLite |
1155	
1156	The handler creates an `imported-<hash>` run, parses the source, appends entries to `traces.jsonl` + `provenance.jsonl`, marks the run `Completed` (skipping the gate), and never writes back to the source. Current coverage is **inventory-level**: it produces a listing/summary but doesn't deeply normalize all fields. Round-trip parity (import → `show <id>` → render comparable to source) is a hardening target — see `docs/goals/2026-05-11-1400-deadreckon-robust-rider.md` §7.
1157

## Summary

Based on my thorough investigation of the codex codebase, "goals" is a **first-class, persistent subsystem** for multi-turn agentic work. Here's the complete map:

### 1. **Code Organization**

**Core Rust crates:**
- `/Users/gdc/codex/codex-rs/core/src/goals.rs` — main lifecycle & accounting engine (350+ lines)
- `/Users/gdc/codex/codex-rs/core/src/tools/handlers/goal/*.rs` — three tools: `create_goal`, `update_goal`, `get_goal`
- `/Users/gdc/codex/codex-rs/state/src/model/thread_goal.rs` — data model & SQLite row mapping
- `/Users/gdc/codex/codex-rs/state/src/runtime/goals.rs` — state-db persistence layer
- `/Users/gdc/codex/codex-rs/core/src/context/goal_context.rs` — runtime prompt injection

**TUI/CLI:**
- `/Users/gdc/codex/codex-rs/tui/src/chatwidget/slash_dispatch.rs` — `/goal` slash-command dispatch
- `/Users/gdc/codex/codex-rs/tui/src/chatwidget/goal_menu.rs` — goal UI menu
- `/Users/gdc/codex/codex-rs/tui/src/app/thread_goal_actions.rs` — goal state mutations

### 2. **User-Facing Surface**

**Slash-command:** `/goal <objective>` (defined in `slash_dispatch.rs:36-37`)

**Agent-callable tools** (three Responses API functions):
- `create_goal(objective: string, token_budget?: i64)` — Creates goal; fails if one exists
- `update_goal(status: "complete")` — **Only way agent marks goal done**; agent cannot pause/resume
- `get_goal()` — Reads current goal state

**UI:** Menu with pause, resume, clear, objective-edit actions; goal status display; budget tracking

**Env/Flags:** Feature-gated (`Feature::Goals` in `tool_config.rs`)

### 3. **Data Model**

**SQLite schema** (`0029_thread_goals.sql`):
```sql
CREATE TABLE thread_goals (
  thread_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
  goal_id TEXT,
  objective TEXT,
  status TEXT CHECK(status IN ('active', 'paused', 'budget_limited', 'complete')),
  token_budget INTEGER,
  tokens_used INTEGER,
  time_used_seconds INTEGER,
  created_at_ms, updated_at_ms
)
```

**Rust struct** (`thread_goal.rs:52-63`):
```rust
pub struct ThreadGoal {
  pub thread_id: ThreadId,
  pub goal_id: String,
  pub objective: String,
  pub status: ThreadGoalStatus,
  pub token_budget: Option<i64>,
  pub tokens_used: i64,
  pub time_used_seconds: i64,
  pub created_at: DateTime<Utc>,
  pub updated_at: DateTime<Utc>,
}
```

**Status enum** (`thread_goal.rs:12-36`): `Active | Paused | BudgetLimited | Complete`

### 4. **Lifecycle: Create → Store → Evaluate → Complete**

**Creation:** User calls `create_goal(objective)` → tool handler validates objective ≤4000 chars → assigns UUID `goal_id` → writes to state-db with `Active` status

**Storage:** One goal per thread (upsert on conflict); `goal_id`, `tokens_used`, `time_used_seconds` auto-updated by runtime

**Evaluation:** Each turn, runtime event loop (`goals.rs:GoalRuntimeEvent`) tracks token deltas & wall-clock time; when budget exhausted → system auto-transitions to `BudgetLimited` status

**Completion:** **Agent-only**, via `update_goal(status="complete")`. Handler (`update_goal.rs:51-56`) enforces: agent cannot pause/resume; agent can only mark `Complete`. System then emits `GOAL_COMPLETED_METRIC` (line 19).

**"Done" gate:** No external signature; the agent's tool call to `update_goal` is the acceptance. Preconditions checked:
- `continuation.md` (lines 30-41): Agent must audit requirements against current state before calling `update_goal`; cannot rely on memory; must verify every requirement with **authoritative evidence**

### 5. **In-Process, No Separate Binary**

All goal logic runs in-process in `codex-rs/core`. No subprocess or external validator. The **semantic gate is the agent's own audit** (continuation.md strictness), not a cryptographic seal.

### 6. **No Signed/Sealed Completion Artifacts**

No nonces, no signatures, no prevent-self-declaration mechanisms. The runtime ensures:
- Agent can only mark `Complete` (not other statuses)
- Completion event is metered (metrics emitted)
- Budget limits are enforced by system (agent cannot bypass)

But **nothing prevents agent from falsely calling `update_goal("complete")`** if it ignores the prompt's audit instructions.

### 7. **Agent Loop Integration**

Goal state drives **prompt injection**. At turn start:
- If goal is `Active`: inject `continuation.md` (full objective + budget + completion audit rules)
- If goal is `BudgetLimited`: inject `budget_limit.md` (wrap up, no new work)
- If goal is `Paused`: agent does not run; user must `/goal resume` (slash-command)

Continuation can resume paused goals via `continue_active_goal_if_idle()` hook (`codex_thread.rs`).

### 8. **Docs & Philosophy**

**Templates** (embedded in binary, `core/src/goals.rs`):
- `templates/goals/continuation.md` — Multi-turn behavior: keep objective whole, audit before marking complete
- `templates/goals/budget_limit.md` — Budget exhaustion: wrap up, no new substantive work
- `templates/goals/objective_updated.md` — Objective changed: treat new objective as ground truth

No standalone `AGENTS.md` describing philosophy, but templates encode the contract: **turn-isolation discipline, evidence-based completion**, persistent across turns.

---

**What "goals" IS:** A persistent, budget-gated, multi-turn task container per thread. User sets a goal via `/goal`; agent pursues it over turns (continuation prompts injected); agent can pause/resume (user-controlled), but only agent can declare completion via `update_goal("complete")` with implied audit. Budget limits auto-trigger system `BudgetLimited` status. All state in SQLite; no external validation.

## Report: Goals Feature in Deadreckon

### 1. **Where Goals-Related Code Lives**

- `/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon-core/src/chain.rs` (lines 75–145) — `ChainStep.goal: String`, `Chain.root_goal: String`, autonomous goal-chaining records
- `/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon-core/src/promotion.rs` — `PromotionManifest.goal: String`, completion flow (lines 16–76)
- `/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon-core/src/docs.rs` (lines 214–1796) — goal text used in turn-doc generation (title from goal at line 1024)

**Runtime & Orchestration:**
- `/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon-runtime/src/turn_loop.rs` (lines 349–596) — `run_acceptance_gate(state)`, `validate_acceptance_marker(state)`, goal rendered in acceptance prompt (lines 690–728), dr-gate invocation (lines 1226–1308)

**CLI & Commands:**
- `/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon/src/main.rs` (lines 213–1010) — `deadreckon run <goal>`, chain plan/extend with step goals, goal string passed to `RunOptions`

**Skills & Documentation:**
- `/Users/gdc/deadreckon/skills/default-coding/SKILL.md` — Markdown skill that owns prose and judgment; loaded at runtime
- `/Users/gdc/deadreckon/docs/goals/` — eight dated goal+rider pairs (e.g., `2026-05-10-1400-deadreckon-build-goal.md`, `2026-05-10-1400-deadreckon-build-rider.md`)

### 2. **User-Facing Surface**

**CLI Commands:**
- `deadreckon run <goal>` — primary entry point; creates durable run state, picks provider, executes turns in sandbox
- `deadreckon chain plan <large-goal> --n <steps>` — split goal into ordered steps (line 866 in main.rs)
- `deadreckon chain extend <run-id> <step-goal>` — add follow-up goal as a child chain step (line 987)
- `deadreckon list [--scope <scope>]` — lists goals with status and metadata
- `deadreckon show <run-id>` — displays goal alongside traces, provenance, artifacts

**Config & Skill Loading:**
- Goal + rider markdown files in `/Users/gdc/deadreckon/docs/goals/` — user writes brief goal, agent loads paired rider (prescriptive detail) at runtime
- Default skill: `/Users/gdc/deadreckon/skills/default-coding/SKILL.md` — loaded per run and recorded in state (DESIGN.md lines 68–69)

### 3. **Data Model**

**Goal Structure:**
- `PipelineState.goal: String` — freeform text, e.g., "Build V0 of deadreckon at /Users/gdc/deadreckon/"
- Task key (hash) derived from goal slug + FNV1a32 (paths.rs:88–99 in AS-BUILT) — two runs with same goal share a lock

**Acceptance Spec (for gate):**
- `/Users/gdc/deadreckon/acceptance.yaml` (optional per run root) — parsed by `gate.rs:455–482`
- Variants: `CargoTest`, `FileExists`, `ContentMatch`, `BuildSuccess`, `Shell`, each with `must_pass` boolean
- Optional vs. required checks: `optional`, `required`, `tests`, `file-exists`, `content-match`, `build-success` sections (gate.rs:463–479)

**Acceptance Marker (signed proof):**
- Struct: `schema_version`, `run_id`, `status` ("pass"), `produced_by` ("dr-gate"), `checked_at`, `working_dir`, `signature`, `check_count`, `checks: Vec<AcceptanceCheckResult>`
- Location: `<run_root>/proofs/turn-acceptance.json`
- Signature: hash over nonce (secret, only dr-gate reads) + marker fields (gate.rs:603–619)

**Chain Structures:**
- `ChainStep { index, goal, status, run_id, applied_sha, fail_reason, max_spend_usd, spend_usd }` (chain.rs:75–112)
- `Chain { chain_id, root_goal, steps: Vec<ChainStep>, ... }` (chain.rs:115–146) — records ordered goal dependencies

### 4. **Goal Lifecycle: Creation → Evaluation → Completion**

**Flow:**

1. **User writes goal** → `deadreckon run "goal text"`
2. **Binary creates state** (`state.rs:create_run`) — allocates `run_id`, task_key, `run_root`, writes `state.json`, writes `gate/nonce` (UUID only dr-gate sees), ensures docs dir
3. **Agent reads goal** from `PipelineState` or turn context; skill (e.g., `default-coding/SKILL.md`) processes it with prose judgment
4. **Agent attempts solution** in turns (per-turn snapshots, traces, provenance written)
5. **Acceptance evaluation** (`turn_loop.rs:349` or line 595) — LLM declares done → runtime invokes `dr-gate` binary as subprocess
6. **`dr-gate` runs checks** (`dr-gate.rs`) — reads `acceptance.yaml` (if present), evaluates `AcceptanceCheck` variants (cargo test, file-exists, content-match, shell, build-success), signs marker with nonce
7. **Marker validated** (`gate.rs:validate_acceptance_marker`) — binary refuses to mark run `Completed` unless marker: ✓ signed with correct nonce, ✓ matches run_id, ✓ produced_by == "dr-gate"
8. **Run promoted** (`promotion.rs:promote_completed_run`) — atomic swap from `working/` → `library/<scope>/<run-id>/`
9. **Runstatus set to `Completed`** — only reachable via Phase(60) + acceptance marker (AS-BUILT §5, line 287)

**Key: Agent cannot self-mark gate.** The nonce is unreadable by agent; any forged marker fails signature check at `gate.rs:133`.

### 5. **Role of dr-gate, Acceptance Markers, Signatures, Nonces**

- **Nonce** (`gate/nonce`): UUID written at run-init by deadreckon binary (state.rs:188); only dr-gate reads it. Agent never sees it.
- **Signature**: HMAC-like hash over nonce + marker fields (gate.rs:603–619). Computed only by dr-gate (`src/bin/dr-gate.rs`).
- **AcceptanceMarker**: Struct written to `proofs/turn-acceptance.json` with `status="pass"`, `produced_by="dr-gate"`, signed marker (gate.rs:141–192).
- **Validation**: deadreckon binary calls `validate_acceptance_marker(state)` (gate.rs:109–139); rejects if signature != expected, run_id mismatches, or produced_by != "dr-gate".
- **Anti-self-attestation**: Agent cannot forge a marker; even if it writes JSON to the marker file, binary detects signature mismatch and blocks completion (gate.rs:134–136, AS-BUILT §8 §17).

### 6. **goal-rider-author Skill**

The skill `goal-rider-author` is referenced in the available skills list but is NOT in `/Users/gdc/deadreckon/skills/`. It is a **Claude Code remote skill** (triggered via `/goal-rider-author` or "draft a goal+rider") that the Claude Code framework provides. It generates goal+rider markdown file pairs using the format seen in `docs/goals/`:

- **Goal** (≤4000 chars): Concise problem statement, references, phase plan, verification checklist, stop condition.
- **Rider** (unbounded): Prescriptive detail with eleven phases, depth-tests-first, exact file paths, hard constraints marked "do not violate," crate dependencies, CLI surface, UX commitments.

Example output in deadreckon repo: `/Users/gdc/deadreckon/docs/goals/2026-05-10-1400-deadreckon-build-{goal,rider}.md`.

### 7. **Philosophy & Distinctive Features**

**DESIGN.md** (lines 1–146) frames the product: unattended long-running tasks, BYOK providers, durable state at every turn, resume-after-crash, full spend/provenance audits.

**AS-BUILT-ARCHITECTURE.md** (§5, §8, §13–15) codifies patterns:
- Two-layer split: Rust binary owns durable invariants; skill (Markdown) owns judgment and prose.
- Phase machine with on-disk `state.json` and gap-numbered phase IDs.
- Atomic promotion: work in `working/`, swapped to `library/` only after gate passes.
- Anti-self-attestation: acceptance markers signed by external `dr-gate` binary; agent cannot forge.
- Per-turn snapshots, provenance (file→prompt lineage), spend tracking, structured traces.

**Distinctive:** 
- Goals are **short text prompts** (e.g., 1–2 sentences); riders are **prescriptive constraint documents** (architecture, must-haves, V0 decisions, layout, verification).
- Goals become **task keys** (slug + FNV hash) → parallel runs with same goal share a lock.
- Chain goals enable **autonomous multi-step decomposition**: `chain plan <goal> --n 4` splits one goal into N ordered steps, each run atomically.
- Acceptance spec (`acceptance.yaml`) is **data-driven** and **provider-agnostic**: checks are file/shell/cargo, not model-specific.

### 8. **Other Distinctive Patterns**

- **Turn-doc checkpoints**: Each turn appends deterministic records to `working/.deadreckon/docs/`, then `run-narrator` skill (if enabled) polish-passes before promotion (DESIGN.md lines 105–109).
- **Provider routing**: goals are provider-agnostic; `--provider anthropic|openai|cli:codex|smoke` selected at run time.
- **Sandbox isolation**: goals run in platform-native sandbox (`sandbox-exec` on macOS, `bwrap` on Linux) by default; `--sandbox auto|none|docker` flag.
- **Run promotion**: only completed + accepted runs atomically copied to `library/`; worktree runs leave `dr/...` branch for review before `apply` (finalize) or `abandon` (discard).

---

**What This Feature IS:** Goals are **unattended coding task prompts** that drive the deadreckon harness from user input through multi-turn agent iteration to signed acceptance and library promotion. A goal is stored in `PipelineState`, hashed into a task key to coordinate parallel work, optionally paired with a prescriptive rider markdown file, decomposed into chained steps for autonomous multi-step work, and **never self-marked complete** — the agent submits work for external `dr-gate` acceptance (required checks: tests, files, shell scripts, cargo build), which signs an unforgeable marker (nonce-based HMAC) that the binary validates before moving the run to `Completed` and promoting it to the library. The architecture treats goals as durable, snapshot-backed, fully audited coding work units that can resume after crashes, undo to any prior turn, and export with full provenance.

# Goals: deadreckon vs codex

Both repos have a real "goals" subsystem, but they sit at opposite ends of a philosophical axis: codex **trusts the agent** to self-declare done with disciplined prompting; deadreckon **distrusts the agent** and forces an external cryptographic gate.

## Side-by-side

| Axis | codex | deadreckon |
|---|---|---|
| Scope of a goal | One per *thread* (interactive chat) | One per *run* (batch/unattended) |
| Persistence | SQLite (`thread_goals` table, migration 0029) | Filesystem (`state.json`, `acceptance.yaml`, `proofs/`) |
| User entry surface | `/goal <objective>` slash-cmd; agent tools `create_goal`/`update_goal`/`get_goal` | `deadreckon run <goal>` CLI + optional goal+rider markdown pair in `docs/goals/` |
| Goal payload | Short objective string (≤4000 chars) | Short goal string **plus** optional prescriptive rider markdown (architecture, constraints, phase plan) |
| Completion gate | Agent calls `update_goal(status="complete")` in-process; runtime accepts the call | External `dr-gate` subprocess evaluates `acceptance.yaml` checks and writes a signed marker; binary re-validates signature |
| Anti-self-attestation | **None.** Prompt (`continuation.md`) tells the agent to audit before marking complete — but nothing stops a false call | **Cryptographic.** Marker is HMAC'd over a per-run nonce in `gate/nonce` that the agent process never sees; forged markers are refused |
| What "done" means | Agent's own audit against the objective text | Executable assertions: `cargo_test`, `file_exists`, `content_match`, `build_success`, `shell` — pass/fail are deterministic |
| Budget enforcement | First-class: `token_budget`, `tokens_used`, `time_used_seconds` tracked per turn; runtime auto-transitions to `BudgetLimited` | `--max-spend-usd` / `--max-wall-seconds` on the run, but no inline goal-status mutation |
| Status model | Enum: `Active / Paused / BudgetLimited / Complete` (user can pause/resume) | Phase machine + `RunStatus`; no user-driven pause, but durable state allows resume-after-crash |
| Decomposition | No multi-goal chaining — one objective per thread | `deadreckon chain plan <goal> --n N` splits one goal into N ordered child runs (`ChainStep`) |
| Provider coupling | Tied to codex's own runtime | Provider-agnostic (`--provider anthropic|openai|cli:codex|smoke`) — codex is one of *our* providers |
| Post-completion | Goal row stays in thread; metrics emitted | Atomic promotion: `working/` → `library/<scope>/<run-id>/` only after signed marker validates |

## What this means

The two systems are solving adjacent but different problems.

**Codex's goals are a chat-session continuity primitive** — "remember what we're working toward across turns, meter the budget, let the user pause." The gate is *epistemic*: the agent reads `continuation.md` each turn and is told to audit before declaring done. If the agent lies, the system has no defense.

**Deadreckon's goals are an unattended-build contract** — "I'm going to leave this running and trust the result." The gate is *mechanical*: tests either pass or they don't, files either exist or they don't, and a nonce the agent can't read signs the proof. The agent literally cannot mark itself done.

A few concrete things deadreckon has that codex doesn't:
- **Rider docs.** Goals are paired with a prescriptive rider (`docs/goals/2026-05-11-1400-deadreckon-primary-flow-rider.md` etc.) generated by the `goal-rider-author` skill — eleven phases, depth-tests-first. Codex has no analog; objective is one string.
- **Executable acceptance spec.** `acceptance.yaml` is data-driven and provider-agnostic. Codex has no externalized "done" definition.
- **Chain decomposition.** `chain plan/extend` for multi-step autonomy. Codex has one goal per thread, period.
- **Atomic promotion + provenance.** A signed-completed run is moved to a library with full file→prompt lineage. Codex keeps state but doesn't promote.

A few things codex has that deadreckon doesn't:
- **Live budget metering inside the goal record.** `tokens_used` / `time_used_seconds` are part of the goal row and drive an automatic `BudgetLimited` state transition with a different prompt template injected. Deadreckon tracks spend on the run, not as a goal-state mutation, and doesn't switch prompt mode when budget gets tight.
- **User-driven pause/resume on the goal itself.** Deadreckon's resume is for crash recovery, not user intent.
- **Per-turn prompt injection from a goal template library** (`continuation.md`, `budget_limit.md`, `objective_updated.md`). Deadreckon's per-turn behavior comes from the skill, not from goal-state-conditioned templates.

## Verdict

Deadreckon is the **stricter, batch-oriented cousin**: better suited to "go build this and I'll check the proof in an hour," weaker at "we're chatting and I want to set a north star for this session."

Codex is the **interactive cousin**: better suited to live multi-turn collaboration with a north star and a budget, weaker at unattended runs where you can't trust the agent's self-report.

The interesting cross-pollination opportunities, if you wanted them:
1. **Pull codex's budget-state prompt switching into deadreckon** — when spend crosses 80%, inject a wrap-up template. Cheap win.
2. **Pull deadreckon's `acceptance.yaml` + signed marker into codex** as an *optional* hard gate for "serious" goals. Codex agents could declare a goal "production-grade," which would require an external check before `update_goal("complete")` is honored.
3. **Pull codex's `Paused` state into deadreckon** so a human can stop a chain mid-flight without killing the run.

```text
# Coding-Agent Harness Landscape vs. deadreckon

## 1. Scored Table

## 2. Top 3 Closest Analogs

**OpenHands.** The most production-grade comparable. It runs as a long-lived agent loop inside a Docker sandbox, persists an immutable event log enabling "replay, recovery, and incremental persistence," and ships lifecycle controls including "pause/resume, sub-agent delegation, and history restore." It is provider-agnostic (LiteLLM-backed). **Overlap with deadreckon:** unattended operation, sandbox, durable resumable state, multi-provider. **Where it differs:** completion is still agent-attested — the agent decides when to stop. There is no `acceptance.yaml`-style declarative oracle, no external gate process, no signed marker, and no atomic working→library promotion. OpenHands also targets interactive/cloud GUI surfaces first; deadreckon is CLI/local-first.

**Plandex.** Closest in *workflow shape*. README quotes: "capable of full autonomy," and "a cumulative diff review sandbox keeps AI-generated changes separate from your project files until they are ready to go." Plans are durable objects ("Context loaded by users or the model… accumulated pending changes") with branch/rewind, and it is BYOK multi-provider. **Overlap:** local-first, BYOK, full-auto mode, durable plans, working-area isolation. **Differs:** "done" is still the agent's call (or a human review). The diff sandbox is for *change isolation*, not *acceptance verification*. No declarative acceptance file, no HMAC marker, no rider/spec pair. Plandex Cloud is winding down (Oct 2025) which strengthens the case for local-first harnesses like deadreckon.

**micro-agent (Builder.io).** Smaller and quieter, but it is the only mainstream project I can verify that operationally *uses tests as the completion oracle*: the developer writes a failing test, the agent iterates until it passes, and the test — not the agent — decides done. **Overlap:** test-as-gate philosophy, declarative-ish spec (the test file *is* the spec, in the spirit of deadreckon's `acceptance.yaml`). **Differs:** no signed marker, no sandboxing, no durable resume, no multi-step rider, no atomic library promotion. Stale (last push 2024-11). It is a philosophical cousin more than a peer.

## 3. Distinctive Gaps (deadreckon-only features I could not find elsewhere)

- **Cryptographically signed completion markers (HMAC over a per-run nonce hidden from the agent).** I searched explicitly for "HMAC", "signed marker", "signed completion" in the agent-harness space and found nothing. Chorus has an admin-verifier role, agent-harness-kit has a "reviewer agent + green health.sh," neosigmaai/auto-harness gates on eval scores, SWE-bench gates on tests — but all of these are policy checks an agent could in principle subvert by writing the artifact themselves. None bind completion to a secret the agent cannot read. This appears to be deadreckon's most novel contribution.
- **Goal + rider markdown pair as a first-class authoring pattern.** The closest matches are MetaGPT's PRD ("`Code = SOP(Team)`"), Goose recipes ("a recipe is a reusable YAML workflow definition that packages a complete task with goals, required extensions, structured inputs, and sub-recipes"), and SWE-agent's single-yaml config. None separate the *terse spine* (goal) from the *prescriptive elaboration* (rider). It's a small but real design idea I didn't see elsewhere.
- **Out-of-process gate binary (`dr-gate`) as a separate trust boundary.** Every other harness I checked runs verification *inside* the agent's process (a reviewer sub-agent, a hook, a tool call). Putting the gate in a separate subprocess holding a secret the agent process never sees is structurally different and pairs with the signed-marker feature.
- **Atomic working/ → library/ promotion** keyed off the verified marker. Plandex has a diff sandbox and Sweep has PR-based isolation, but the promotion gate is human or agent, not a verified artifact.

## 4. Adjacent-but-different

- **Aider** (~45k, Apache-2.0). The reference *interactive* AI pair-programmer; with `--yes`/`--auto-test`/`--auto-lint` it edges toward unattended, and it can re-run tests on edit, but it's fundamentally a human-in-the-loop tool. Worth knowing for prompt and diff-application techniques.
- **SWE-bench** (~4.9k, MIT). Not a coding agent — it's the canonical eval *harness* with Docker-isolated test runs ("SWE-bench uses Docker for reproducible evaluations"). It is the strongest existing precedent for "tests decide done," but it is a benchmark scoring rig, not a long-running agent runner. deadreckon's `dr-gate` is closer in spirit to SWE-bench's harness than to any of the agents themselves.
- **AutoGen / CrewAI** (~58k / ~51k). Multi-agent orchestration *frameworks*, not coding agents. They give you reviewer/critic roles and YAML/Pydantic task specs, but no sandbox, no durable run state out of the box, and certainly no signed completion. Useful to know as the framework layer deadreckon explicitly is *not*.
- **Chorus-AIDLC** and **agent-harness-kit**. Newer, smaller projects explicitly using the words "agent harness," with reviewer/approval gates and acceptance criteria. They are the closest *conceptual* neighbors to deadreckon outside the top-3 — worth watching, but neither has a cryptographic completion binding, and both still resolve "done" via an in-process role (reviewer agent / admin user) rather than a trust-boundary-separated verifier.

## Bottom line

The signed-marker / HMAC-over-hidden-nonce completion pattern is, as far as I can verify on GitHub today, **unique to deadreckon**. The goal+rider authoring split appears to be unique too. The rest of deadreckon's surface area (unattended runs, sandbox, durable resume, multi-provider, declarative spec, atomic promotion) has prior art but no single project assembles all of them; OpenHands and Plandex are the most complete assemblies, and neither makes the agent-cannot-self-attest move.
```

Research GitHub for open-source coding-agent harnesses that are comparable to "deadreckon" (a local Rust harness I'm working on). I need you to find the landscape and score each project against the axes that make deadreckon distinctive.

## What deadreckon is, briefly
A local-first Rust harness for **unattended, long-running coding tasks**. User writes a goal (optionally paired with a "rider" — a prescriptive markdown spec); the agent runs in a sandbox over many turns; an **external `dr-gate` subprocess** evaluates a declarative `acceptance.yaml` (cargo test, file_exists, content_match, shell checks) and writes a **cryptographically signed marker** (HMAC over a per-run nonce the agent can never see). The agent literally cannot self-declare done — forged markers are refused. Completed runs are atomically promoted from a `working/` directory to a `library/`. Provider-agnostic (Anthropic, OpenAI, Codex CLI, etc.). Durable state, crash-resume, optional `chain plan` for multi-step decomposition.

## What to find
Search GitHub for open-source projects that are doing **any** of the following, and report which ones overlap most with deadreckon:

1. **Autonomous / unattended coding agents** — meant to run for hours without a human in the loop (not interactive chat-coders like Cursor or Continue.dev, which need a human at every step). Examples to start from: OpenHands (formerly OpenDevin), SWE-agent, smol-developer, gpt-engineer, MetaGPT, Plandex, Aider's `--auto` modes, Sweep, micro-agent, AutoCodeRover, Goose (Block), AutoGen, CrewAI, Devon. There are probably others.
2. **Harnesses with an external verification gate** — i.e., the agent doesn't decide "done"; a separate process or test suite does. SWE-bench evaluation harnesses are an example; the SWE-bench scaffolds (princeton-nlp/SWE-bench, sweep-ai) are relevant. Anything that ties completion to test-suite pass rather than agent self-report.
3. **Anti-self-attestation / signed completion artifacts** — extremely rare; this is deadreckon's most unusual feature. Search for it; report if you find nothing.
4. **Goal + rider / declarative-spec patterns** — agents that take a spec document and a brief and proceed unattended. Plandex's plans, OpenHands' state, MetaGPT's PRD-driven flow are candidates.
5. **Provider-agnostic local-first harnesses** — runs locally, BYOK across multiple model providers (not SaaS). Aider, Goose, OpenHands all qualify.
6. **Sandboxed execution + durable run state + resume-after-crash** — long-running agents with serializable state.

## How to do the research
- Use WebSearch and WebFetch.
- Start with GitHub topic pages: `topic:ai-agent`, `topic:coding-agent`, `topic:autonomous-agent`, `topic:llm-agent`. Also search GitHub for keywords like "acceptance gate" "external verifier" "agent harness" "autonomous coding".
- For each project that looks promising, fetch its README and skim for: completion semantics (who decides done?), state model, sandbox, multi-provider support, license, last-commit date (don't bother with dead projects unless they pioneered something distinctive).
- Don't trust your own training-cutoff memory of these projects — fetch the actual current README. Several of these have evolved a lot in 2024-2026.

## Output format
A markdown report under ~1000 words with:

1. **A scored table.** Columns: project, GitHub URL, stars (approx), license, last activity, then ✓/✗/partial for each of: unattended, external gate, signed completion, declarative spec, multi-provider, durable state, sandbox.
2. **Top 3 closest analogs**, with a paragraph each: what they do, where they overlap with deadreckon, where they differ. Be honest — if no one else has the signed-marker pattern, say so.
3. **Distinctive gaps**: features of deadreckon that you found nowhere else in the landscape. (My guess: the signed marker is unique; the goal+rider markdown pair pattern may be too.)
4. **Adjacent-but-different**: 2-3 projects worth knowing about even though they're solving a different problem (e.g., interactive chat coders, SWE-bench eval scaffolds).

Be specific. Quote a sentence or two from each project's README to back the claim. Skip projects you can't actually verify on GitHub.

```text
## Key Projects and Concepts

Agent harnesses for Claude and Codex include control-plane-grade implementations with policy gates, verification/evidence loops, memory, and auditable execution, with the Claude Code harness featuring hook-enforced dual review and state-machine gates that survive context compaction.

### Verification and Approval Patterns

Chorus is an agent harness for requirements-to-delivery with task DAGs, sub-agent orchestration, proof of work, and human approval gates where "AI proposes, humans verify".

Agent-harness-kit is a provider-agnostic scaffolding kit for running structured multi-agent workflows with a shared structure including a task backlog, defined workflow, persistent log of every action, and a health gate that must be green before any work begins.

The reviewer agent verifies all acceptance criteria are met, approves or blocks tasks, and runs a health check before approving.

### Gate and Safety Mechanisms

Harmonist is a multi-agent framework where protocol enforcement is a mechanical gate with IDE-level hooks checking every code-changing turn for required reviewers, memory updates, and supply-chain integrity, demonstrating deterministic harness constraints that even frontier models cannot override.

Auto-harness gates all changes by requiring them to pass both the eval suite and full test score gate before commitment.
```

```text
Based on the search results, here's what I found about OpenHands runtime sandbox, Docker, durable state, and agent resume capabilities:

## Docker Sandbox Runtime

The Docker sandbox runs the agent server inside a Docker container and is the default and recommended option for most users. OpenHands is built around an execution environment (a sandbox) so an agent can safely run commands and tools, with a Docker-sandboxed runtime environment that includes a shell and browsing capability to support realistic developer-like interaction patterns.

## Durable State Management

Reliably deploying autonomous agents in production requires system foundations—including durable state management, safe execution in a sandbox, and consistent behavior across environments ranging from local to containerized cloud deployments. OpenHands uses an immutable event log for event sourcing of state that enables replay, recovery, and incremental persistence.

## Agent Resume and Lifecycle Control

The OpenHands SDK adds flexible lifecycle control including pause/resume, sub-agent delegation, and history restore, along with built-in QA instrumentation for production reliability.

## Workspace Architecture

Remote Workspace preserves the same interface but delegates all operations over HTTP to an Agent Server, with concrete sponsors including a containerized server (DockerWorkspace) or an API-managed runtime (APIRemoteWorkspace).

The search results show that OpenHands provides comprehensive support for containerized execution with state management capabilities suitable for production deployments.
```

```text
Plandex is capable of full autonomy—it can load relevant files, plan and implement changes, execute commands, and automatically debug. Configurable autonomy allows users to go from full auto mode to fine-grained control depending on the task. In full auto mode, Plandex can independently handle end-to-end tasks, such as debugging a browser app or building features from scratch.

## Durable State & Sandbox

A cumulative diff review sandbox keeps AI-generated changes separate from your project files until they are ready to go. Command execution is controlled so you can easily roll back and debug. The diff sandbox with rewind and branch-style recovery is a meaningful workflow advantage for teams that care about not trashing a repo while experimenting with autonomous agents.

## 2026 Status

Plandex features a diff review sandbox, full auto mode, and smart context management up to 2M tokens. However, Plandex Cloud is winding down as of October 3, 2025 and is no longer accepting new users, with the docs directing users toward self-hosted or local mode instead, with Docker or their own server and their own model-provider API keys.
```

```text
## Chorus Agent Harness Overview

Chorus is an agent harness — the infrastructure that wraps around LLM agents to manage session lifecycle, task state, sub-agent orchestration, observability, and failure recovery. It lets multiple AI Agents (with fine-grained, configurable permissions) and humans collaborate through the full workflow from requirements to delivery.

## Proof of Work & Acceptance Criteria

Chorus includes task DAGs, sub-agent orchestration (Agent Teams), proof of work, and human approval gates.

The system implements a structured approach to acceptance criteria verification. Chorus features a dual-track verification system — developer self-check + admin verification per criterion. There's a new AcceptanceCriterion Prisma model as an independent table, with chorus_report_criteria_self_check and chorus_mark_acceptance_criteria MCP tools.

Dev Agent self-checks and Admin reviews each acceptance criterion independently, with structured pass/fail evidence for every item.

## GitHub Resources

The main Chorus project is available on GitHub at **github.com/Chorus-AIDLC/Chorus**, along with related integrations like the OpenCode-Chorus plugin at **github.com/etnperlong/opencode-chorus**. The system implements a complete workflow that reverses the conversation (AI proposes, humans verify) through the workflow: Idea ──> Proposal ──> [Document + Task DAG] ──> Execute ──> Verify ──> Done.
```

```text
# Gating Mechanism in auto-harness

The harness gates completion through a **three-step process** without signed markers. It's an **eval framework** (not a coding agent). Verbatim:

> "gating.py — three-step gate: eval suite + full test val_score + suite promotion"

The specific steps are:

1. **Regression suite**: Tasks in `suite.json` must pass at ≥ threshold (default 80%)
2. **Full test**: Full benchmark on test split; mean reward must meet or exceed the best score recorded so far
3. **Suite promotion**: Previously-failing tasks that now pass are added to the suite

The framework explicitly notes: "Steps 1 and 2 run sequentially; Step 2 always runs regardless of Step 1's outcome."
```

## 1. Scored Table

## 2. Top 3 Closest Analogs

**OpenHands.** The most production-grade comparable. It runs as a long-lived agent loop inside a Docker sandbox, persists an immutable event log enabling "replay, recovery, and incremental persistence," and ships lifecycle controls including "pause/resume, sub-agent delegation, and history restore." It is provider-agnostic (LiteLLM-backed). **Overlap with deadreckon:** unattended operation, sandbox, durable resumable state, multi-provider. **Where it differs:** completion is still agent-attested — the agent decides when to stop. There is no `acceptance.yaml`-style declarative oracle, no external gate process, no signed marker, and no atomic working→library promotion. OpenHands also targets interactive/cloud GUI surfaces first; deadreckon is CLI/local-first.

**Plandex.** Closest in *workflow shape*. README quotes: "capable of full autonomy," and "a cumulative diff review sandbox keeps AI-generated changes separate from your project files until they are ready to go." Plans are durable objects ("Context loaded by users or the model… accumulated pending changes") with branch/rewind, and it is BYOK multi-provider. **Overlap:** local-first, BYOK, full-auto mode, durable plans, working-area isolation. **Differs:** "done" is still the agent's call (or a human review). The diff sandbox is for *change isolation*, not *acceptance verification*. No declarative acceptance file, no HMAC marker, no rider/spec pair. Plandex Cloud is winding down (Oct 2025) which strengthens the case for local-first harnesses like deadreckon.

**micro-agent (Builder.io).** Smaller and quieter, but it is the only mainstream project I can verify that operationally *uses tests as the completion oracle*: the developer writes a failing test, the agent iterates until it passes, and the test — not the agent — decides done. **Overlap:** test-as-gate philosophy, declarative-ish spec (the test file *is* the spec, in the spirit of deadreckon's `acceptance.yaml`). **Differs:** no signed marker, no sandboxing, no durable resume, no multi-step rider, no atomic library promotion. Stale (last push 2024-11). It is a philosophical cousin more than a peer.

## 3. Distinctive Gaps (deadreckon-only features I could not find elsewhere)

- **Cryptographically signed completion markers (HMAC over a per-run nonce hidden from the agent).** I searched explicitly for "HMAC", "signed marker", "signed completion" in the agent-harness space and found nothing. Chorus has an admin-verifier role, agent-harness-kit has a "reviewer agent + green health.sh," neosigmaai/auto-harness gates on eval scores, SWE-bench gates on tests — but all of these are policy checks an agent could in principle subvert by writing the artifact themselves. None bind completion to a secret the agent cannot read. This appears to be deadreckon's most novel contribution.
- **Goal + rider markdown pair as a first-class authoring pattern.** The closest matches are MetaGPT's PRD ("`Code = SOP(Team)`"), Goose recipes ("a recipe is a reusable YAML workflow definition that packages a complete task with goals, required extensions, structured inputs, and sub-recipes"), and SWE-agent's single-yaml config. None separate the *terse spine* (goal) from the *prescriptive elaboration* (rider). It's a small but real design idea I didn't see elsewhere.
- **Out-of-process gate binary (`dr-gate`) as a separate trust boundary.** Every other harness I checked runs verification *inside* the agent's process (a reviewer sub-agent, a hook, a tool call). Putting the gate in a separate subprocess holding a secret the agent process never sees is structurally different and pairs with the signed-marker feature.
- **Atomic working/ → library/ promotion** keyed off the verified marker. Plandex has a diff sandbox and Sweep has PR-based isolation, but the promotion gate is human or agent, not a verified artifact.

## 4. Adjacent-but-different

- **Aider** (~45k, Apache-2.0). The reference *interactive* AI pair-programmer; with `--yes`/`--auto-test`/`--auto-lint` it edges toward unattended, and it can re-run tests on edit, but it's fundamentally a human-in-the-loop tool. Worth knowing for prompt and diff-application techniques.
- **SWE-bench** (~4.9k, MIT). Not a coding agent — it's the canonical eval *harness* with Docker-isolated test runs ("SWE-bench uses Docker for reproducible evaluations"). It is the strongest existing precedent for "tests decide done," but it is a benchmark scoring rig, not a long-running agent runner. deadreckon's `dr-gate` is closer in spirit to SWE-bench's harness than to any of the agents themselves.
- **AutoGen / CrewAI** (~58k / ~51k). Multi-agent orchestration *frameworks*, not coding agents. They give you reviewer/critic roles and YAML/Pydantic task specs, but no sandbox, no durable run state out of the box, and certainly no signed completion. Useful to know as the framework layer deadreckon explicitly is *not*.
- **Chorus-AIDLC** and **agent-harness-kit**. Newer, smaller projects explicitly using the words "agent harness," with reviewer/approval gates and acceptance criteria. They are the closest *conceptual* neighbors to deadreckon outside the top-3 — worth watching, but neither has a cryptographic completion binding, and both still resolve "done" via an in-process role (reviewer agent / admin user) rather than a trust-boundary-separated verifier.

## Bottom line

The signed-marker / HMAC-over-hidden-nonce completion pattern is, as far as I can verify on GitHub today, **unique to deadreckon**. The goal+rider authoring split appears to be unique too. The rest of deadreckon's surface area (unattended runs, sandbox, durable resume, multi-provider, declarative spec, atomic promotion) has prior art but no single project assembles all of them; OpenHands and Plandex are the most complete assemblies, and neither makes the agent-cannot-self-attest move.

Research is in. Key takeaways:

## The headline finding

**The signed-marker / hidden-nonce completion pattern appears unique to deadreckon.** The agent searched GitHub explicitly for "HMAC", "signed completion", "external verifier" in the agent-harness space and found nothing comparable. Every other harness ultimately lets the agent (or a sub-agent the agent can call) write the completion artifact. Binding completion to a secret the agent process can never read is a structural move no one else has made.

## Closest analogs

**OpenHands** (All-Hands-AI, ~73k★) — the most production-grade peer. Runs long, sandboxes in Docker, has a durable event log with replay/recovery, BYOK multi-provider via LiteLLM. **Differs**: completion is agent-attested. No `acceptance.yaml`, no external gate process, no atomic promotion.

**Plandex** (~15k★) — closest in *workflow shape*. Full-auto mode, BYOK, "cumulative diff review sandbox keeps AI changes separate until ready." **Differs**: the diff sandbox is for change isolation, not acceptance verification. Done is still the agent's call. (Their cloud is winding down Oct 2025, which arguably strengthens deadreckon's local-first positioning.)

**micro-agent** (BuilderIO, ~4.3k★) — the *philosophical* cousin. Failing test as the oracle: agent iterates until the test passes; the test, not the agent, decides done. **Differs**: no sandbox, no durable resume, no signed artifact, stale since 2024-11.

## What's actually distinctive about deadreckon

1. **Signed marker over hidden nonce** — unique on GitHub as of this research.
2. **Out-of-process `dr-gate` binary as a trust boundary** — every other harness runs verification *inside* the agent process (reviewer sub-agent, hook, tool call). Putting it in a subprocess with a secret the agent can't see is a different security posture.
3. **Goal + rider markdown pair** — terse spine + prescriptive elaboration. MetaGPT's PRD, Goose recipes, and SWE-agent's YAML config all bundle these together; nobody splits them.
4. **Atomic working→library promotion keyed off the verified marker** — Plandex has change isolation, Sweep has PRs, but promotion-gated-by-verified-artifact is novel.

The rest of deadreckon's surface (sandbox, durable resume, multi-provider, declarative spec) has prior art — **OpenHands and Plandex assemble the most of it**, but neither makes the agent-cannot-self-attest move.

## Worth knowing but solving a different problem

- **SWE-bench** (~4.9k★) — not an agent, but the canonical "tests decide done" eval harness. Closest *spiritual* precedent for `dr-gate`.
- **Aider** (~45k★) — reference interactive coder; `--yes --auto-test --auto-lint` edges toward unattended, but fundamentally human-in-the-loop.
- **AutoGen / CrewAI** — multi-agent orchestration *frameworks*, not coding agents. Reviewer/critic roles but no sandbox, no durable runs, no signed completion. The layer deadreckon explicitly is not.

## Two newer small projects worth tracking
- **Chorus-AIDLC** — uses "agent harness" terminology, has reviewer/criterion gates.
- **agent-harness-kit** — reviewer agent + green `health.sh`, sqlite-backed state.

_**Agent (claude-opus-4-7 2026-05-12 22:28:51Z)**_

_**Agent (claude-opus-4-7 2026-05-12 22:29:13Z)**_

Sure. It's three concepts stacked. Let me unpack each, then show why the combination is novel.

## 1. "Marker"

When a deadreckon run finishes, the harness writes a small JSON file:

```
<run-root>/proofs/turn-acceptance.json
```

It contains fields like `run_id`, `status: "pass"`, `produced_by: "dr-gate"`, `checked_at`, and the list of check results. This file is the **claim** that the run succeeded. The Rust binary refuses to mark a run `Completed` unless this file exists and validates. (See `validate_acceptance_marker` at `gate.rs:109-139`.)

So the marker is the "ticket out" — without it the run can't terminate cleanly.

## 2. "Signed"

The marker has a `signature` field. It's computed by hashing the marker's fields *plus a secret*:

```rust
// gate.rs:603-619
fn marker_signature(run_root: &Path, marker: &AcceptanceMarker) -> Result<String> {
    let nonce = std::fs::read_to_string(&nonce_path)...;
    let mut hasher = DefaultHasher::new();
    nonce.trim().hash(&mut hasher);
    marker.schema_version.hash(&mut hasher);
    marker.run_id.hash(&mut hasher);
    // ...all marker fields and check results...
    Ok(format!("{:016x}", hasher.finish()))
}
```

When the harness validates a marker, it recomputes the signature the same way and refuses any marker whose stored signature doesn't match (`gate.rs:132-137`). This is the same idea as HMAC: if you don't know the secret, you can't produce a valid signature, and if you tamper with any field, the signature stops matching.

So "signed" means: **only something that knew the secret could have produced this file.**

## 3. "Hidden nonce"

The "secret" here is a per-run random value (a nonce) stored at:

```
<run-root>/gate/nonce
```

It's written once when the run is created, by the parent harness process. Crucially, it lives **outside the working directory the agent operates in**. The agent's sandbox profile doesn't grant read access to it. The agent process literally cannot open this file. (`gate.rs:16` defines the path as `gate/nonce`, separate from `working/` where the agent lives.)

Only the `dr-gate` subprocess — which is started by the harness, not by the agent — reads the nonce when it writes a marker.

So "hidden" doesn't mean obscured or hard-to-find; it means **structurally inaccessible to the entity being audited**.

## Putting it together: the threat model

Imagine the simpler design — agent calls a `done()` tool, harness marks the run complete. The agent can lie. It can claim done when tests fail, when files weren't written, when the goal wasn't met. Codex's `update_goal("complete")` is exactly this design (with a strongly-worded prompt asking the agent to audit itself, which it might or might not honor).

Now imagine a stricter design — the harness runs the tests itself before accepting `done()`. Better, but: who runs the test runner? If the agent can write files in the working directory, it can sometimes manipulate test outcomes. And if the verification logic lives in the same process as the agent, the agent might tool-call its way around it.

deadreckon's design closes both holes:

| Layer | Defense |
|---|---|
| Agent can't claim done in-process | The harness shells out to a separate `dr-gate` binary that runs the actual checks |
| Agent can't fabricate the marker file | Even if the agent writes a perfect-looking `turn-acceptance.json`, validation recomputes the signature and rejects it without the nonce |
| Agent can't read the nonce and sign its own marker | The nonce file is outside the agent's sandbox-readable paths |
| Agent can't tamper with a real marker after dr-gate writes it | Any field change breaks the signature |

Two of the four tests in `gate.rs` specifically prove this (`rejects_agent_written_marker_with_wrong_run_id` at line 638, `self_attest_attempt_fails` at line 857).

## Why it's unique

Most "autonomous coding agent" harnesses on GitHub stop at one of these earlier points:

- **OpenHands, Aider, Plandex**: agent decides done. Trust the prompt.
- **micro-agent**: test failure decides done, but the agent can write the tests, so it's only as strict as the human-supplied test fixture.
- **Sweep, agent-harness-kit**: a reviewer agent or `health.sh` decides done — but the reviewer is just more LLM, callable by the same agent, and the health script lives in the same filesystem the agent can edit.
- **SWE-bench**: tests-as-oracle, but it's a benchmark scoring rig run *after* the agent finishes by a separate human-controlled process. Not a continuous gate inside a live agent loop.

What deadreckon does that the research couldn't find elsewhere: **bake the trust boundary into the agent loop itself, with a cryptographic binding to a secret the agent can never see, so the agent can run unattended for hours and you still know its self-report is meaningful.** That's the move.

The practical payoff: you can leave a deadreckon run going overnight and the worst case is "it failed to complete and you find that out in the morning." Not "it lied to you and you don't find out until you ship broken code." For an unattended-build harness, that's the whole game.

```
    │                  │   ◄── "done"   │  emits Action::Done  │
    └────────┬─────────┘                └──────────────────────┘
             │                                ▲ can read: working/
             │                                ✗ cannot read: gate/nonce
             │
             │ spawns subprocess
             ▼
    ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │ dr-gate binary                                           │
    │                                                          │
    │  1. read acceptance.yaml                                 │
    │  2. run each check (cargo test, file_exists, shell, …)   │
    │  3. read gate/nonce       ◄── has filesystem access      │
    │  4. compute signature =                                  │
    │        hash(nonce ‖ run_id ‖ checks ‖ status ‖ …)        │
    │  5. write proofs/turn-acceptance.json with signature     │
    │                                                          │
    └──────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────┘
                               │
                               ▼
    ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │ parent harness — validate_acceptance_marker()            │
    │                                                          │
    │   read marker JSON                                       │
    │   read gate/nonce                                        │
    │   recompute expected_signature                           │
    │                                                          │
    │   if marker.signature != expected     → REJECT           │
    │   if marker.run_id    != this_run     → REJECT           │
    │   if marker.produced_by != "dr-gate"  → REJECT           │
    │   if marker.status    != "pass"       → REJECT           │
    │                                                          │
    │   else → mark run Completed, promote working/ → library/ │
    └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘


  attack:  agent fabricates  proofs/turn-acceptance.json
           ├── status=pass, produced_by=dr-gate, signature="????"
           └── validator recomputes with nonce → mismatch → REJECT
                  ↑
              agent never saw the nonce, so it can't produce
              a signature that will validate
```

The three things that make this work, in one sentence each:

- **`gate/nonce` lives outside the agent's sandbox-readable paths** — structural, not just policy.
- **`dr-gate` is a separate subprocess spawned by the parent**, not a tool the agent can call.
- **The signature binds every field of the marker to the nonce** — tamper with any field after the fact and validation fails.

_**Agent (claude-opus-4-7 2026-05-12 23:01:01Z)**_

_**Agent (claude-opus-4-7 2026-05-12 23:01:05Z)**_

- At run-init Deadreckon writes a per-run random secret (a nonce) to a path the agent's sandbox can't read
- When the agent says "done", the parent harness shells out to the separate dr_gate subprocess — the agent can't call dr_gate as a tool
- dr_gate executes your acceptance criteria (tests, file checks, shell commands), then signs the result by hashing the outcome together with the hidden nonce, and writes that signed marker to disk
- Even if the agent fabricates its own marker file claiming success, validation recomputes the signature with the nonce and rejects any marker the agent could have written
- Only a marker signed by dr_gate (with the right nonce, run_id, and "pass" status) lets the run terminate — otherwise the loop keeps going
- On a valid signed marker the run is atomically promoted from `working/` to `library/`, with full provenance; on failure the agent gets another turn to try again
- Net effect: you can walk away from a long run and trust the "done" signal when you come back, because the agent literally cannot produce it on its own

more simply

_**Agent (claude-opus-4-7 2026-05-12 23:01:25Z)**_

- Deadreckon hides a secret token from the agent at the start of the run
- When the agent claims "done", a separate watchdog process (dr_gate) runs your acceptance checks
- If they pass, dr_gate stamps the result with the secret — the agent can't forge that stamp
- No valid stamp = the agent keeps working
- Valid stamp = the run is done, for real

21

21	
22	1. **You write "done" in plain English.** deadreckon compiles it into executable checks — tests that must pass, files that must exist, scripts that must succeed.
23	2. **The agent runs in an isolated worktree**, inside a sandbox. Your real checkout is never touched.

30	## Why this matters
31	
32	- **You can leave a long run going and trust the result.** The agent can't lie its way out of the gate.
