35	- **If anything dies — terminal, network, the model — the run survives.** Attach from a new terminal, resume from any turn, undo a bad step.
36	
37	## Why "deadreckon"?
38	
39	Dead reckoning is navigation without perfect visibility: start from a known
40	position, keep a continuous record of movement, and use that record to know
41	where you are now.
42	
43	That is the problem with unattended coding agents. The model is probabilistic,
44	the task can run for a long time, context is partial, and the terminal may be
45	gone by the time you inspect the result. deadreckon keeps the course anyway:
46	every turn writes state, spend, traces, provenance, snapshots, docs, and
47	acceptance evidence.
48	
49	The name is the contract: do not trust a final answer alone. Navigate agent work
50	by evidence.
51	
52	## Why This Exists
53	
54	Agentic coding CLIs are good at the inner loop: talk to a model, inspect files, run commands, edit code, and produce a patch. Amp, Rovo Dev, Cursor CLI, Codex, Claude Code, Aider, deepseek-tui, GitHub Copilot CLI, and similar tools are racing on model UX, tool UX, context handling, and terminal/editor ergonomics.
55	
56	deadreckon focuses on the layer around that CLI: the unattended run lifecycle.
57	
58	The painful part of unattended coding is different:
59	
60	- Where exactly did the agent run?
61	- What did it spend?
62	- Which files did each turn touch?
63	- Can I attach after closing my laptop?
64	- Can I kill it without leaving orphaned processes?
65	- Can I resume after a crash?
66	- Can I undo turn 7 without rolling back the whole project?
67	- Can I prove the agent did not mark its own work as accepted?
68	- Can I apply the result only after I inspect it?
69	
70	deadreckon is built around those questions. It treats an agentic CLI as the worker, then adds the control plane that makes unattended work reviewable, recoverable, auditable, and safe to apply.
71	
72	## The Printing Press Contract
73	
74	deadreckon borrows a simple idea from the CLI Printing Press pattern: split
75	judgment from enforcement.
76	
77	The agentic CLI and Markdown skills own the judgment layer: what to inspect,
78	what to try, what to edit, and when to say the work is done. The Rust binary owns
79	the enforcement layer: state, locks, sandboxes, provider routing, cancellation,
80	snapshots, provenance, spend, traces, gates, promotion, and recovery.
81	
82	That split matters. The agent can write code, but it cannot forge completion,
83	skip the audit trail, bypass run state, or silently publish its own work.
84	
85	## The Unique Feature Set
86	
87	### Your Checkout Is Never Touched (Isolated Worktrees By Default)
88	
89	In a git repo, `deadreckon run` creates a separate `git worktree` on a `dr/...` branch under `~/.deadreckon/worktrees/`. Your checkout is left untouched until you explicitly run:
90	
91	```bash
92	deadreckon apply <run-id>
93	```
94	
95	Run ids accept unique prefixes, and most commands also accept `latest` for the
96	newest run in the current project.
97	
98	You can also run in copy mode, fresh mode, or explicit in-place mode:
99	
100	```bash
101	deadreckon run "goal" --from .
102	deadreckon run "goal" --fresh
103	deadreckon run "goal" --in-place --i-know-its-a-lot
104	```
105	
106	### Use The Agent CLI You Already Trust
107	
108	deadreckon routes turns through configurable providers. Today, the first-class local CLI adapters are:
109	
110	- `cli:codex`
111	- `cli:claude-code`
112	
113	It also supports direct model routes:
114	
115	- `anthropic`
116	- `openai`
117	- OpenAI-compatible endpoints
118	- `--smoke` for keyless local verification
119	
120	That means subscription users can route through supported local agentic CLIs, while API users can route through direct HTTP providers. The CLI does the coding; deadreckon owns the run boundary around it.
121	
122	### Crash-Proof: Every Turn Is Saved To Disk
123	
124	Each run writes a complete local record under `~/.deadreckon/runstate/`:
125	
126	```text
127	state.json
128	history.json
129	events.jsonl
130	traces.jsonl
131	spend.jsonl
132	provenance.jsonl
133	snapshots/turn-<N>/
134	proofs/turn-acceptance.json
135	working/ or promoted library artifact
136	```
137	
138	If the terminal dies, the run state is still there. If a provider call completes, the trace is there. If a tool edits a file, the provenance is there.
139	
140	### Walk Away, Attach From Any Terminal
141	
142	Start a run, walk away, then attach from another terminal:
143	
144	```bash
145	deadreckon attach latest
146	```
147	
148	The TUI shows compact run status, phase, goal, working directory, per-turn timer,
149	spend or context telemetry, provider/tool activity, generated files, process
150	status, and completion actions. Completed runs can toggle a styled Markdown
151	rendering of `RUN-NARRATIVE.md` directly in the main panel.
152	
153	Detach without killing the run:
154	
155	```text
156	Ctrl-D
157	```
158	
159	### Set A Budget And A Time Limit, Then Walk Away
160	
161	Every provider response appends a spend record and updates totals. API routes track token cost. Subscription CLI routes can be capped by wall-clock time.
162	
163	```bash
164	deadreckon run "large refactor" --max-spend 15
165	deadreckon run "large refactor" --max-wall-seconds 1800
166	```
167	
168	High spend requires explicit confirmation, so scripts do not accidentally launch expensive runs.
169	
170	### Undo A Single Bad Turn Without Losing The Rest
171	
172	deadreckon snapshots the working directory at turn boundaries:
173	
174	```bash
175	deadreckon undo --run <run-id>
176	deadreckon undo --run <run-id> --turn 3
177	```
178	
179	This is not just `git reset`. It works against the run's own snapshot trail and records the undo in the run trace.
180	
181	### Write "Done" In English, Verified By A Watchdog
182	
183	Tell deadreckon what success looks like in plain language. It compiles your sentence into executable checks that an independent watchdog runs:
184	
185	```bash
186	deadreckon done "build, load in a browser, and show no console errors"
187	deadreckon done add "users can save drawings"
188	deadreckon done check
189	deadreckon run "finish the app"
190	```
191	
192	`deadreckon run` and `deadreckon chain run` prompt interactively when a project has no acceptance file yet. Generated files live under `.deadreckon/acceptance.yaml`, `.deadreckon/acceptance.md`, and optional helper scripts in `.deadreckon/acceptance/`.
193	
194	**Why the watchdog matters.** Completion requires a marker file written by the separate `dr-gate` binary. That binary holds a secret (a per-run nonce) that lives outside the agent's sandbox-readable paths. It hashes the secret together with the check results to sign the marker. deadreckon refuses any marker whose signature doesn't validate against that secret — so even if the agent fabricates a perfect-looking "I'm done" file, it gets rejected.
195	
196	The agent runs the code. The watchdog decides whether the code passed. They are different processes with different filesystem reach. The agent cannot become the watchdog.
197	
198	If no acceptance file is configured, the default is the working directory exists and `cargo test` passes (when `Cargo.toml` is present).
199	
200	You can still edit the compiled YAML directly:
201	
202	```yaml
203	name: notes check
204	checks:
205	  - kind: file_exists
206	    path: "{working_dir}/notes.md"
207	  - kind: content_match
208	    path: "{working_dir}/notes.md"
209	    pattern: "dead reckoning"
210	  - kind: build_success
211	    cwd: "{working_dir}"
212	```
213	
214	Supported executable check kinds are `cargo_test`, `file_exists`, `content_match`, `build_success`, and `shell`. `content_match` treats `pattern` as a regex when valid, with substring fallback for simple text.
215	
216	### Get An Auditable Artifact, Not A Transcript
217	
218	deadreckon records which model/tool call touched which files, then writes self-documenting artifacts for the completed run:
219	
220	```bash
221	deadreckon doc <run-id>
222	deadreckon doc <run-id> --kind as-built
223	deadreckon doc <run-id> --kind decisions
224	deadreckon doc <run-id> --kind delta
225	```
226	
227	Each accepted run produces a review packet:
228	
229	- `RUN-NARRATIVE.md` explains what happened.
230	- `RUN-AS-BUILT.md` captures the subsystem shape after the run.
231	- `RUN-DECISIONS.md` records meaningful decisions.
232	- `AS-BUILT-DELTA.md` proposes architecture-doc updates when the run is broad enough.
233	- `manifest.json` records the promoted artifact identity and provenance hash.
234	
235	Agentic CLIs usually leave you with a patch and a transcript. deadreckon turns
236	the session into a local published artifact you can inspect, materialize, extend,
237	or apply.
238	
239	### Resume, Kill, Extend, Or Export Any Run
240	
241	Runs are lifecycle objects, not one terminal session:
242	
243	```bash
244	deadreckon list
245	deadreckon status
246	deadreckon show latest
247	deadreckon kill latest
248	deadreckon resume latest
249	deadreckon resume latest --from-turn 2
250	deadreckon extend latest "add tests and polish the UI"
251	deadreckon finish latest
252	deadreckon export latest --dest ./finished-project
253	deadreckon cleanup --completed
254	```
255	
256	Resume reconstructs history from durable traces and ignores incomplete trailing trace entries.
257	
258	### Autonomous Chains For Multi-Step Work
259	
260	Some tasks are too big for one goal. Chains let you break work into ordered steps that run end-to-end, with the same gate enforcement and the same lifecycle commands per step:
261	
262	```bash
263	deadreckon chain plan "ship a working SaaS billing flow" --n 4
264	deadreckon chain run latest
265	deadreckon chain attach latest
266	deadreckon chain kill latest
267	```
268	
269	Each chain step is a real run with its own signed acceptance gate. If a step fails its gate, the chain stops there — later steps don't start. Killing a chain cascades to whatever step is live. The attach TUI shows the whole chain timeline, not just the current turn, so you can see where you are in the plan without leaving the dashboard.
270	
271	You can also extend a finished run into a follow-up step instead of planning the whole chain up front:
272	
273	```bash
274	deadreckon chain extend latest "add billing webhooks and retry logic"
275	```
276	
277	## The Mental Model
278	
279	```text
280	your repo
281	  |
282	  | deadreckon done "what 'finished' looks like, in English"
283	  | deadreckon run  "what to build"
284	  v
285	isolated worktree or copy   ◄── your real checkout untouched
286	  |
287	  | provider route: cli:codex, cli:claude-code, anthropic, openai, ...
288	  v
289	sandboxed turn loop         ◄── agent works here
290	  |
291	  | every turn: trace, spend, provenance, snapshot, docs
292	  | check fails? agent gets another turn
293	  v
294	dr-gate watchdog            ◄── separate process, holds hidden nonce
295	  |                              agent CANNOT produce a valid marker
296	  | checks pass + signature valid?
297	  v
298	promoted artifact           ◄── narrative, decisions, file lineage
299	  |
300	  | inspect, doc, apply, discard, extend, export, cleanup
301	  v
302	your branch or library
303	```
304	
305	For multi-step work, `deadreckon chain` wraps this whole loop and runs N of them in order, stopping on the first gate failure.
306	
307	deadreckon owns the boring but load-bearing parts: state, locks, sandboxes, provider routing, cancellation, snapshots, provenance, gates, and promotion.
308	
309	The agent owns the coding work.
310	
311	## The Trust Contract
312	
313	With deadreckon, `completed` means more than "the agent stopped." It means:
314	
315	- the run state was persisted
316	- the work happened in an isolated workspace
317	- spend and traces were written
318	- file provenance was recorded
319	- snapshots exist for rollback
320	- run docs were generated
321	- `dr-gate` signed acceptance
322	- the artifact was promoted atomically
323	
324	That is the difference between an agent transcript and an auditable run.
325	
326	## Quickstart
327	
328	Build the release binary:
329	
330	```bash
331	cargo build --release
332	```
333	
334	Initialize local config:
335	
336	```bash
337	./target/release/deadreckon init
338	```
339	
340	Run a task:
341	
342	```bash
343	./target/release/deadreckon run "make a realtime chess app"
344	```
345	
346	Attach to the run:
347	
348	```bash
349	./target/release/deadreckon attach <run-id>
350	```
351	
352	Inspect the result:
353	
354	```bash
355	./target/release/deadreckon show <run-id>
356	./target/release/deadreckon doc <run-id>
357	```
358	
359	Apply a completed worktree run:
360	
361	```bash
362	./target/release/deadreckon apply latest --autostash --cleanup
363	```
364	
365	## Keyless Smoke Test
366	
367	Use `--smoke` to prove the harness works without API keys or subscription-backed CLIs:
368	
369	```bash
370	DEADRECKON_HOME=$PWD/.deadreckon-smoke \
371	  ./target/release/deadreckon run "tiny hello rust" \
372	  --smoke \
373	  --sandbox none \
374	  --max-spend 1
375	```
376	
377	This still exercises the real turn loop, sandbox dispatch, snapshots, spend records, traces, provenance, docs, and acceptance gate. The only fake part is the provider response.
378	
379	## Normal Coding Run
380	
381	After `init`, the default path in a git repo is:
382	
383	```bash
384	deadreckon run "make a full task productivity tracker in nodejs that allows me to manage my day"
385	deadreckon attach latest
386	deadreckon status
387	deadreckon doc latest
388	deadreckon apply latest --autostash --cleanup
389	```
390	
391	`run` prints the run id and attach command immediately:
392	
393	```text
394	started run <short-id> (<full-id>)
395	attach: deadreckon attach <short-id>
396	```
397	
398	Before creating state or files, `run` prints a preview showing the mode, branch, base ref, and worktree path. Use `--preview` to print the preview and exit.
399	
400	## Provider Configuration
401	
402	Examples:
403	
404	```bash
405	deadreckon init --provider cli:codex --sandbox auto --max-spend 10 --no-confirm
406	deadreckon init --provider cli:claude-code --sandbox auto --max-spend 10 --no-confirm
407	deadreckon init --provider anthropic --api-key "$ANTHROPIC_API_KEY" --sandbox auto --max-spend 10 --no-confirm
408	deadreckon init --provider openai --api-key "$OPENAI_API_KEY" --sandbox auto --max-spend 10 --no-confirm
409	```
410	
411	Inspect or edit config:
412	
413	```bash
414	deadreckon config get defaults.provider
415	deadreckon config provider
416	deadreckon config provider cli:codex
417	deadreckon config model
418	deadreckon config model gpt-5.1-codex --provider cli:codex
419	deadreckon config set defaults.max_spend 15
420	deadreckon config set defaults.sandbox auto
421	deadreckon config set providers.anthropic.api_key "$ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"
422	```
423	
424	Before a run, `deadreckon run --preview "goal"` shows the provider route and
425	model that will be used. For one run, override both directly:
426	
427	```bash
428	deadreckon run "goal" --provider cli:codex --model gpt-5.1-codex
429	deadreckon run "goal" --provider cli:claude-code --model sonnet
430	```
431	
432	Runtime config defaults to:
433	
434	```text
435	~/.deadreckon/config.toml
436	```
437	
438	Set `DEADRECKON_HOME` for isolated local runs or tests.
439	
440	## Sandbox Backends
441	
442	Supported backends:
443	
444	```text
445	auto
446	sandbox-exec
447	bwrap
448	docker
449	none
450	```
451	
452	`auto` chooses `sandbox-exec` on macOS when available and `bwrap` on Linux when available. `docker` is opt-in. `none` is explicit and warns because it is unsafe for real unattended work.
453	
454	Check the current machine:
455	
456	```bash
457	deadreckon doctor
458	```
459	
460	## Compared With Agentic Coding CLIs
461	
462	deadreckon is not a replacement for agentic CLIs like Amp, Rovo Dev, Cursor CLI, Codex, Claude Code, Aider, deepseek-tui, or GitHub Copilot CLI. It is the supervisor you put around that class of tool when the task is too long, risky, or expensive for "run the agent in my checkout and hope I can reconstruct what happened."
463	
464	| Operational concern | Agentic CLI alone | deadreckon supervising the CLI |
465	|---|---|---|
466	| Workspace safety | Often runs where you start it | Creates an isolated worktree by default and leaves your checkout untouched |
467	| Long-running attach | Usually tied to the current terminal session | Run state is durable; attach from another terminal later |
468	| Process control | Kill/resume behavior varies by tool | Tracks child PIDs, kills live work, resumes from durable state |
469	| Spend control | Token/cost visibility varies by provider | Writes `spend.jsonl`, tracks totals, enforces spend and wall-clock caps |
470	| Undo | Usually git-level or manual | Snapshots every turn and restores a specific turn with `deadreckon undo` |
471	| Provenance | Conversation history may not map cleanly to file changes | Records model/tool/file linkage in `provenance.jsonl` |
472	| Observability | Tool logs are tool-specific | Writes normalized `events.jsonl`, `traces.jsonl`, spend, docs, and run state |
473	| Done criteria | The agent may declare itself done | Requires a signed `dr-gate` marker before promotion |
474	| Applying work | Patch review/apply flow is tool-specific | `apply`, `discard`, `export`, `extend`, and `cleanup` are first-class lifecycle actions |
475	| Multi-run coordination | Usually left to the operator | Scope/task locks prevent conflicting same-task runs |
476	
477	Use the agentic CLI for intelligence. Use deadreckon for isolation, supervision, evidence, recovery, and promotion.
478	
479	## Command Surface
480	
481	```text
482	init          create local config
483	config        inspect or edit config keys
484	run           start an unattended coding run
485	attach        open the live dashboard
486	status/next   show the current project's latest run and next action
487	list          show current-project runs by default; --all shows every scope
488	show          inspect state, lineage, spend, files
489	doc           print or export run documentation
490	finish        choose apply or export from the completed run mode
491	apply         apply a completed worktree run to your branch
492	keep          alias for apply

 # deadreckon
 
-**The control plane for unattended agentic coding CLIs.**
+**A harness around the agent CLI you already use, so you can actually walk away.**
 
-deadreckon runs long coding tasks the way you wish agentic CLIs already did: in an isolated workspace, with durable state, live attach, spend and wall-clock caps, per-turn undo, provenance, traces, self-documenting run artifacts, and a signed acceptance gate before anything is promoted.
+Codex, Claude Code, Aider, and the rest are good at writing code. They are not built to run unattended for hours and tell you, honestly, whether the work got done. deadreckon is.
 
-It is not trying to out-code Amp, Rovo Dev, Cursor CLI, Codex, Claude Code, Aider, deepseek-tui, GitHub Copilot CLI, or the next terminal agent. Use the agentic CLI you already trust. deadreckon wraps it in the missing operational harness.
+You bring the agent CLI you already trust. You tell deadreckon what "done" looks like in plain English. It runs the work in an isolated sandbox, saves every turn, and uses a separate watchdog process to decide when the job is actually finished — a watchdog the agent cannot fool.
 
 ```bash
-deadreckon run "replace the legacy billing flow with Stripe Checkout"
+deadreckon done "users can sign up, log in, and save a drawing"
+deadreckon run "build the app"
+# walk away, attach later from any terminal
 deadreckon attach latest
-deadreckon status
-deadreckon doc latest
-deadreckon finish latest
-deadreckon apply latest --autostash --cleanup
 ```
 
+## How it works
+
+1. **You write "done" in plain English.** deadreckon compiles it into executable checks — tests that must pass, files that must exist, scripts that must succeed.
+2. **The agent runs in an isolated worktree**, inside a sandbox. Your real checkout is never touched.
+3. **Every turn is saved** — state, spend, traces, file provenance, snapshots — so you can attach, kill, resume, undo, or audit any moment.
+4. **A separate watchdog process (`dr-gate`) decides when the work is done.** It holds a secret the agent process cannot read, and signs the result with that secret. The agent cannot forge the signature, so it cannot mark its own work as accepted.
+5. **If the checks fail, the loop keeps going.** The agent gets another turn. When the watchdog finally signs off for real, the run is atomically promoted to a reviewable artifact — narrative, decisions, file provenance, full audit trail.
+
+The loop is the product. The agent CLI does the coding. deadreckon decides when "done" actually means done.
+
+## Why this matters
+
+- **You can leave a long run going and trust the result.** The agent can't lie its way out of the gate.
+- **Use whichever agent CLI you prefer.** Claude Code, Codex, Aider, or direct Anthropic / OpenAI API — deadreckon supervises any of them.
+- **You get an auditable artifact, not a chat transcript.** Narrative, decisions, file lineage, spend, traces — all on disk.
+- **If anything dies — terminal, network, the model — the run survives.** Attach from a new terminal, resume from any turn, undo a bad step.
+

 Dead reckoning is navigation without perfect visibility: start from a known

31	
32	- **You can leave a long run going and trust the result.** The agent can't lie its way out of the gate.
33	- **Use whichever agent CLI you prefer.** Claude Code, Codex, Cursor CLI, or direct Anthropic / OpenAI API — deadreckon supervises any of them.
34	- **You get an auditable artifact, not a chat transcript.** Narrative, decisions, file lineage, spend, traces — all on disk.
35	- **If anything dies — terminal, network, the model — the run survives.** Attach from a new terminal, resume from any turn, undo a bad step.
36	
37	## Why "deadreckon"?
38	
39	Dead reckoning is navigation without perfect visibility: track every move so you know where you are now. Unattended agents are the same problem — long task, partial context, the terminal may be gone when you look back. The name is the contract: don't trust the final answer, navigate by evidence.
40	
41	The questions deadreckon is built to answer:
42	
43	- Where did the agent run, and what did it spend?
44	- Can I attach after closing my laptop?
45	- Can I undo turn 7 without rolling back the whole project?
46	- Can I prove the agent did not mark its own work as accepted?
47	
48	## Features
49	
50	### Your Checkout Is Never Touched (Isolated Worktrees By Default)
51	
52	In a git repo, `deadreckon run` creates a separate `git worktree` on a `dr/...` branch under `~/.deadreckon/worktrees/`. Your checkout is left untouched until you explicitly run:
53	
54	```bash
55	deadreckon apply <run-id>
56	```
57	
58	Run ids accept unique prefixes, and most commands also accept `latest` for the
59	newest run in the current project.
60	
61	You can also run in copy mode, fresh mode, or explicit in-place mode:
62	
63	```bash
64	deadreckon run "goal" --from .
65	deadreckon run "goal" --fresh
66	deadreckon run "goal" --in-place --i-know-its-a-lot
67	```
68	
69	### Use The Agent CLI You Already Trust
70	
71	Route turns through whichever provider you prefer:
72	
73	- **Local CLIs** (subscription): `cli:claude-code`, `cli:codex`
74	- **Direct APIs** (BYOK): `anthropic`, `openai`, OpenAI-compatible endpoints
75	- **Smoke** (keyless): `--smoke` for local verification
76	
77	The CLI does the coding; deadreckon owns the run boundary around it.
78	
79	### Crash-Proof: Every Turn Is Saved To Disk
80	
81	Every turn writes state, traces, spend, file provenance, and a working-directory snapshot under `~/.deadreckon/runstate/`. If the terminal dies, attach from another. If the run itself crashes, resume from the last completed turn.
82	
83	### Walk Away, Attach From Any Terminal
84	
85	```bash
86	deadreckon attach latest
87	```
88	
89	The TUI shows live status, current step, spend, recent file edits, and provider activity. Completed runs render `RUN-NARRATIVE.md` inline. Press `Ctrl-D` to detach without killing the run.
90	
91	### Set A Budget And A Time Limit, Then Walk Away
92	
93	Every provider response appends a spend record and updates totals. API routes track token cost. Subscription CLI routes can be capped by wall-clock time.
94	
95	```bash
96	deadreckon run "large refactor" --max-spend 15
97	deadreckon run "large refactor" --max-wall-seconds 1800
98	```
99	
100	High spend requires explicit confirmation, so scripts do not accidentally launch expensive runs.
101	
102	### Undo A Single Bad Turn Without Losing The Rest
103	
104	deadreckon snapshots the working directory at turn boundaries:
105	
106	```bash
107	deadreckon undo --run <run-id>
108	deadreckon undo --run <run-id> --turn 3
109	```
110	
111	This is not just `git reset`. It works against the run's own snapshot trail and records the undo in the run trace.
112	
113	### Write "Done" In English, Verified By A Watchdog
114	
115	Tell deadreckon what success looks like in plain language. It compiles your sentence into executable checks that an independent watchdog runs:
116	
117	```bash
118	deadreckon done "build, load in a browser, and show no console errors"
119	deadreckon done add "users can save drawings"
120	deadreckon done check
121	deadreckon run "finish the app"
122	```
123	
124	`deadreckon run` and `deadreckon chain run` prompt interactively when a project has no acceptance file yet. Generated files live under `.deadreckon/`.
125	
126	**Why the watchdog matters.** The watchdog holds a secret the agent process cannot read. It stamps the result with that secret. Without a valid stamp, the run can't terminate — and the agent can't produce the stamp itself.
127	
128	If no acceptance file is configured, the default is "the working directory exists and `cargo test` passes" (when `Cargo.toml` is present).
129	
130	You can still edit the compiled YAML directly:
```
</details></tool-use>

```text
130	You can still edit the compiled YAML directly:
131	
132	```yaml
133	name: notes check
134	checks:
135	  - kind: file_exists
136	    path: "{working_dir}/notes.md"
137	  - kind: content_match
138	    path: "{working_dir}/notes.md"
139	    pattern: "dead reckoning"
140	  - kind: build_success
141	    cwd: "{working_dir}"
142	```
143	
144	Supported executable check kinds are `cargo_test`, `file_exists`, `content_match`, `build_success`, and `shell`. `content_match` treats `pattern` as a regex when valid, with substring fallback for simple text.
145	
146	### Get An Auditable Artifact, Not A Transcript
147	
148	deadreckon records which model/tool call touched which files, then writes self-documenting artifacts for the completed run:
149	
150	```bash
151	deadreckon doc <run-id>
152	deadreckon doc <run-id> --kind as-built
153	deadreckon doc <run-id> --kind decisions
154	deadreckon doc <run-id> --kind delta
155	```
156	
157	Each accepted run produces a review packet:
158	
159	- `RUN-NARRATIVE.md` explains what happened.
160	- `RUN-AS-BUILT.md` captures the subsystem shape after the run.
161	- `RUN-DECISIONS.md` records meaningful decisions.
162	- `AS-BUILT-DELTA.md` proposes architecture-doc updates when the run is broad enough.
163	- `manifest.json` records what was built and from what.
164	
165	Agentic CLIs usually leave you with a patch and a transcript. deadreckon turns
166	the session into a local published artifact you can inspect, materialize, extend,
167	or apply.
168	
169	### Resume, Kill, Extend, Or Export Any Run
170	
171	Runs are lifecycle objects, not one terminal session:
172	
173	```bash
174	deadreckon list
175	deadreckon status
176	deadreckon show latest
177	deadreckon kill latest
178	deadreckon resume latest
179	deadreckon resume latest --from-turn 2
180	deadreckon extend latest "add tests and polish the UI"
181	deadreckon finish latest
182	deadreckon export latest --dest ./finished-project
183	deadreckon cleanup --completed
184	```
185	
186	Resume reconstructs history from durable traces and ignores incomplete trailing trace entries.
187	
188	### Autonomous Chains For Multi-Step Work
189	
190	Some tasks are too big for one goal. Chains let you break work into ordered steps that run end-to-end, with the same gate enforcement and the same lifecycle commands per step:
191	
192	```bash
193	deadreckon chain plan "ship a working SaaS billing flow" --n 4
194	deadreckon chain run latest
195	deadreckon chain attach latest
196	deadreckon chain kill latest
197	```
198	
199	Each chain step is a real run with its own signed acceptance gate. If a step fails its gate, the chain stops there — later steps don't start. Killing a chain cascades to whatever step is live. The attach TUI shows the whole chain timeline, not just the current turn, so you can see where you are in the plan without leaving the dashboard.
200	
201	You can also extend a finished run into a follow-up step instead of planning the whole chain up front:
202	
203	```bash
204	deadreckon chain extend latest "add billing webhooks and retry logic"
205	```
206	
207	## The Mental Model
208	
209	```text
210	your repo
211	  |
212	  | deadreckon done "what 'finished' looks like, in English"
213	  | deadreckon run  "what to build"
214	  v
215	isolated worktree or copy   ◄── your real checkout untouched
216	  |
217	  | provider route: cli:codex, cli:claude-code, anthropic, openai, ...
218	  v
219	sandboxed turn loop         ◄── agent works here
220	  |
221	  | every turn: trace, spend, provenance, snapshot, docs
222	  | check fails? agent gets another turn
223	  v
224	dr-gate watchdog            ◄── separate process, holds hidden nonce
225	  |                              agent CANNOT produce a valid marker
226	  | checks pass + signature valid?
227	  v
228	promoted artifact           ◄── narrative, decisions, file lineage
229	  |
230	  | inspect, doc, apply, discard, extend, export, cleanup
231	  v
232	your branch or library
233	```
234	
235	For multi-step work, `deadreckon chain` wraps this whole loop and runs N of them in order, stopping on the first gate failure.
236	
237	The agent owns the coding. deadreckon owns the boundary.
238	
239	## Quickstart
240	
241	Build once:
242	
243	```bash
244	cargo build --release
245	```
246	
247	The binary is `./target/release/deadreckon`. Add it to your `PATH` or alias it; the rest of this README just says `deadreckon`.
248	
249	Configure and run a task end-to-end:
250	
251	```bash
252	deadreckon init --provider cli:claude-code --sandbox auto --max-spend 10
253	
254	deadreckon done   "users can sign up, log in, and save a drawing"
255	deadreckon run    "build the app"
256	deadreckon attach latest    # watch live, Ctrl-D to detach
257	deadreckon doc    latest    # read the narrative once done
258	deadreckon apply  latest --autostash --cleanup
259	```
260	
261	`run` prints the run id and attach command immediately, and shows a preview of mode, branch, base ref, and worktree path before creating anything. Use `--preview` to print the preview and exit.
262	
263	### Try It Without API Keys
264	
265	```bash
266	DEADRECKON_HOME=$PWD/.deadreckon-smoke \
267	  deadreckon run "tiny hello rust" --smoke --sandbox none --max-spend 1
268	```
269	
270	The provider response is faked, but every other moving part — turn loop, sandbox, snapshots, spend, traces, gate — is real.
271	
272	## Configuration
273	
274	Switch providers, models, or defaults:
275	
276	```bash
277	deadreckon init --provider cli:codex --sandbox auto --max-spend 10
278	deadreckon init --provider anthropic --api-key "$ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"
279	deadreckon config provider cli:claude-code
280	deadreckon config model sonnet --provider cli:claude-code
281	deadreckon config set defaults.max_spend 15
282	```
283	
284	Override per run:
285	
286	```bash
287	deadreckon run "goal" --provider cli:codex --model gpt-5.1-codex
288	deadreckon run --preview "goal"     # show route and model, don't start
289	```
290	
291	Runtime config lives at `~/.deadreckon/config.toml`. Set `DEADRECKON_HOME` for isolated local runs or tests.
292	
293	### Sandbox Backends
294	
295	| Backend | What it is |
296	|---|---|
297	| `auto` | Picks the right native sandbox for your OS (default) |
298	| `sandbox-exec` | macOS native |
299	| `bwrap` | Linux native (bubblewrap) |
300	| `docker` | Opt-in container sandbox |
301	| `none` | Off — unsafe for real unattended work |
302	
303	Check what your machine supports with `deadreckon doctor`.
304	
305	## Compared With Agentic Coding CLIs
306	
307	deadreckon doesn't replace Claude Code, Codex, or Cursor CLI — it supervises them. Use deadreckon when the task is too long, risky, or expensive to "run the agent in my checkout and hope I can reconstruct what happened."
308	
309	| Operational concern | Agentic CLI alone | deadreckon supervising the CLI |
310	|---|---|---|
311	| Workspace safety | Often runs where you start it | Creates an isolated worktree by default and leaves your checkout untouched |
312	| Long-running attach | Usually tied to the current terminal session | Run state is durable; attach from another terminal later |
313	| Process control | Kill/resume behavior varies by tool | Tracks child PIDs, kills live work, resumes from durable state |
314	| Spend control | Token/cost visibility varies by provider | Writes `spend.jsonl`, tracks totals, enforces spend and wall-clock caps |
315	| Undo | Usually git-level or manual | Snapshots every turn and restores a specific turn with `deadreckon undo` |
316	| Provenance | Conversation history may not map cleanly to file changes | Records model/tool/file linkage in `provenance.jsonl` |
317	| Observability | Tool logs are tool-specific | Writes normalized `events.jsonl`, `traces.jsonl`, spend, docs, and run state |
318	| Done criteria | The agent may declare itself done | Requires a signed `dr-gate` marker before promotion |
319	| Applying work | Patch review/apply flow is tool-specific | `apply`, `discard`, `export`, `extend`, and `cleanup` are first-class lifecycle actions |
320	| Multi-run coordination | Usually left to the operator | Scope/task locks prevent conflicting same-task runs |
321	
322	Use the agentic CLI for intelligence. Use deadreckon for isolation, supervision, evidence, recovery, and promotion.
323	
324	## Command Surface
325	
326	Core lifecycle:
327	
328	```text
329	init          create local config
330	config        inspect or edit config keys
331	run           start an unattended coding run
332	attach        open the live dashboard
333	status        latest run and next action for this project
334	list          list runs (current project; --all for every scope)
335	show          inspect state, lineage, spend, files
336	doc           print or export run documentation
337	apply         apply a completed worktree run to your branch
338	abandon       remove a worktree run and temporary branch
339	materialize   copy a completed artifact to a normal directory
340	extend        continue from a completed run
341	resume        continue an interrupted run
342	kill          stop a live run and child processes
343	undo          restore a previous turn snapshot
344	cleanup       clean abandoned, stale, or completed worktrees
345	finish        choose apply or export from completed run
346	import        normalize histories from other coding tools
347	doctor        check config, providers, sandboxes, disk, runtime
348	```
349	
350	Aliases: `keep` → `apply`, `discard` → `abandon`, `export` → `materialize`, `prune` → `cleanup`, `follow-up` → `extend`, `continue` → `resume`, `stop` → `kill`, `next` → `status`.
351	
352	## Verification
353	
354	Full local verification:
355	
356	```bash
357	make verify
358	```
359	
360	Useful targeted checks:
361	
362	```bash
363	make build
364	make smoke
365	make doctor
366	STRESS_SECONDS=30 make stress
367	```
368	
369	The workspace test suite covers provider routing, mock OpenAI-compatible runs, CLI-provider wrappers, kill/resume behavior, signed gates, snapshots, provenance/trace linkage, worktree/copy/in-place modes, lifecycle actions, docs generation, and multi-run locking.
370	
371	## Status
372	
373	deadreckon is alpha software. The core lifecycle — isolated runs, signed gates, durable state, undo, docs, and apply — is implemented and tested.
374	
375	The V1 candidate list is deliberately short. The next big feature is explicit sub-agent forking:
376	
377	```text
378	deadreckon fork <run-id> --prompt "..."
379	```
